prompt:
You are a senior typographer and information designer. You lay out data tables for publication. You judge layouts by looking at the rendered result as a whole: what the table is for, how a reader scans and compares it, which columns belong together or play the same role, proportion and rhythm across columns, a clear hierarchy of headers and groups, whether rows read as units, whether words, numbers and identifiers stay intact, and how text and white space are distributed. Fewer lines or a shorter table is not automatically better, and neither is equal widths or symmetry; decide case by case and say why.

Table: השוואת דירות להשכרה בתל אביב (language he, right-to-left: column 1 is on the RIGHT).
Grid: 5 columns × 7 rows. Row headers: yes (first logical column identifies each row).
Per-column content facts (content px at 13px font, excluding padding):
  col 1: header "שכונה" · longest unbreakable word 58px · one-line width 76px
  col 2: header "מחיר" · longest unbreakable word 37px · one-line width 90px
  col 3: header "חדרים" · longest unbreakable word 37px · one-line width 37px
  col 4: header "קומה" · longest unbreakable word 37px · one-line width 122px
  col 5: header "הערות" · longest unbreakable word 70px · one-line width 941px
Each column also has 21px of padding+border, so a column given width w px shows w−21 px of text.
Available width: 584px (the dashed pink box = the reader's viewport). The column widths you choose must sum to at most 583px.
Fixed: content, font, 13px font size, padding, borders, colours, alignment. You control ONLY the column widths.

Your understanding so far: {"purpose":"Compare rental apartments in Tel Aviv by neighborhood, monthly price, size, floor and descriptive notes.","reading":"Readers scan the neighborhood names to identify listings, compare the numeric attributes across rows, then read the notes for details and tradeoffs.","groups":["Neighborhood identifies each listing; price and rooms are the primary comparison fields.","Floor and elevator availability describe accessibility; the floor cell combines both.","Notes contain longer qualitative details and benefit most from flexible width."],"keep_intact":["Neighborhood names where possible, especially multiword names.","Prices and their currency symbols; room counts and decimal values.","Floor numbers and short floor expressions."],"may_wrap":["Long notes can wrap naturally between words.","Elevator descriptions can wrap after the floor information.","The monthly price qualifier can wrap if necessary; note wrapping may already set the row height."]}

The first image is the one-line content overview. The other images are real browser renders of your current designs:
Design r1A: widths [97, 85, 58, 85, 258] · table 584×616px · row heights [33, 94, 94, 94, 94, 94, 114] · column headers wrapped 0/5 · tallest cell 5 lines · mid-word splits 0
Design r1B: widths [97, 111, 58, 85, 232] · table 584×616px · row heights [33, 94, 94, 94, 94, 94, 114] · column headers wrapped 0/5 · tallest cell 5 lines · mid-word splits 0
Design r1C: widths [97, 85, 58, 93, 250] · table 584×616px · row heights [33, 94, 94, 94, 94, 94, 114] · column headers wrapped 0/5 · tallest cell 5 lines · mid-word splits 0

Look carefully at each render as a whole and in detail. For each design say what works and what is visually wrong, and WHY it happens (which width causes it). Then propose up to 3 improved designs: refine the most promising, fix the problems you saw, and try a new idea if an important alternative is unexplored. If no design can be meaningfully improved, set "done": true and return no new designs.
Reply ONLY JSON: {"critique":[{"design":"name","good":"","problems":"","cause":""}],"done":false,"designs":[{"name":"short-name","widths":[int px],"change":"what you changed and why"}]}
